title: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China
description: HANGZHOU, CHINA - APRIL 23: A view of DeepSeek logo at a mall on April 23, 2026 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province of China. DeepSeek launched a preview o
body: HANGZHOU, CHINA - APRIL 23: A view of DeepSeek logo at a mall on April 23, 2026 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province of China. DeepSeek launched a preview of its V4 model, expanding its open-source AI lineup on April 24. (Photo by Long Wei/VCG via Getty Images)Vcg | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesThe Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies. Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported.The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense. Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities. The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

schema.headline: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China

title: BlackRock, GIC among investors chasing Indian telecom major Jio's IPO as anchor bids top $26 billion
description: A Jio Platforms Ltd. logo at a news conference ahead of the company's listing ceremony at Reliance Corporate Park in Mumbai, India, Thursday, Oct. 15,
body: A Jio Platforms Ltd. logo at a news conference ahead of the company's listing ceremony at Reliance Corporate Park in Mumbai, India, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIndia's Jio Platforms has seen the anchor investor quota for its initial public offering oversubscribed more than 30 times, according to a source familiar with the matter, drawing bids from top asset managers including BlackRock, Capital Group and GIC. The country's largest telecommunications and digital services company, backed by Meta and Google, plans to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through India's largest ever IPO in rupee terms.According to the source, who is not allowed to speak on the matter due to legal restrictions, the company's anchor book received total bids worth 2.5 trillion rupees ($26.3 billion) for the 81.1 billion rupee anchor book portion.Jio Platforms, in a release on Monday, said it had finalized the allocation of 72.47 million equity shares to anchor investors at 1,119 rupees a share, at the upper range of the price band. The anchor book is a portion of the total fundraise set aside for large institutional investors before the IPO opens for public bidding. Some other major institutional investors who have been allocated shares include India's state-owned insurance firm Life Insurance Corporation, Fidelity Investments, JPMorgan Asset Management and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.The Jio Platforms IPO will be open to the public from Wednesday through Friday. Jio Platforms, owned by Reliance Industries, has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider. The IPO price values the company at around $108 billion — lower than the valuations of over $130 billion floated a year ago.

schema.headline: BlackRock, GIC among investors chasing Indian telecom major Jio's IPO as anchor bids top $26 billion

title: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments
description: BERLIN, GERMANY - OCTOBER 19: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang toast with drinks while on stage at the Invest In Germany
body: BERLIN, GERMANY - OCTOBER 19: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang toast with drinks while on stage at the Invest In Germany Summit to announce a strategic cooperation between the German government, NVIDIA and a group of German companies in artificial intelligence capacity for Germany industry on October 19, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. The project includes a significant investment by Germany in powerful NVIDIA chips. (Photo by Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images)Nadja Wohlleben | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesNvidia is increasing its investments in Europe's artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI.The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker's nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, as announced at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday.The four startups are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. However, Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments.Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare, while Avelios Medical builds AI-powered hospital management software. Mirelo develops AI models that generate audio for videos, while Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites.The announcement comes as Germany seeks to accelerate AI adoption across its industrial sector, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying the country aims to become a leader in integrating AI into key sectors.Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country's economy, named manufacturing, machinery and the automotive industry for integrating AI. He also urged Germany's small- and medium-sized businesses to capitalize on the data they already hold. "Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data," Merz said. "This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies."Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed Merz's remarks while highlighting Germany's expertise in manufacturing, mathematics and science, saying that AI would strengthen rather than replace the country's industrial capabilities. "AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability," Huang said, describing the technology as a new instrument for businesses.Nvidia is also expanding its collaboration with the German federal government and its "Industry 4.0 Platform," bringing together representatives from government, industry, research and trade associations, to accelerate the adoption of industrial AI. On Monday, the government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia to advance AI models for industrial applications.Earlier in the day, Siemens had also announced new AI solutions developed with Nvidia at its factory in Erlangen, Germany. Siemens said the technologies could reduce engineering work involved in preparing production by up to 85%, while AI-powered production planning could cut costs by as much as 20%.Huang had also visited France last week, where he announced investments in four French startups and met with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss AI development. The Nvidia boss is scheduled to deliver a keynote address in Berlin on Wednesday.

schema.headline: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments

title: JD Vance refrains from endorsing Israeli leader Netanyahu as Trump offers praise
description: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks during a midterm campaign rally at the LevelUp Training Complex on Oct. 15, 2026 in Monroe, Michigan.Pool | Getty
body: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks during a midterm campaign rally at the LevelUp Training Complex on Oct. 15, 2026 in Monroe, Michigan.Pool | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesU.S. Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after President Donald Trump offered his backing for the leader's reelection bid next week.  "The president has the most effective endorsement in American or international political history," Vance said in an interview on Mark Halperin's 2WAY Tonight published Monday. "I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on in the midterms," he said. Vance said he was not criticizing Netanyahu: "I'm not anti-endorsing him. I'm not pro-endorsing him," he said, adding that "I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections." Those remarks diverge from the approach by President Donald Trump, who gave the Israeli prime minister his backing in the election next week. Trump on Sunday praised Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, on Truth Social as "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran." In a social media post, Netanyahu thanked Trump for his "tremendous support and work together." Vance has weighed in on foreign politics before. He campaigned in Budapest in April to publicly endorse then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban's reelection bid. Orban was later voted out after 16 years in power. Last year in Munich for a security conference, Vance met Alice Weidel, the leader of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party, which Elon Musk was also boosting at the time. The Israeli vote next week will be the first national election since Hamas attacked Israel in late 2023. The comments also come as U.S. public support for Israel, historically strong among both Republicans and Democrats, has fallen sharply. There has also been vigorous debate in America about the Netanyahu-led government's response to the Hamas attack.In June, Vance said that Israel has almost no friends left in the world and should think hard before turning on the one it has.

schema.headline: JD Vance refrains from endorsing Israeli leader Netanyahu as Trump offers praise

title: 'Cannot play hide and seek': Minister's warning over haze sends Singapore agricultural stocks lower
description: A container ship is seen docked at the PSA Tanjong Pagar terminal port in Singapore on October 16, 2026, as the country continues to be shrouded in ha
body: A container ship is seen docked at the PSA Tanjong Pagar terminal port in Singapore on October 16, 2026, as the country continues to be shrouded in haze caused by fires in Indonesia. Toxic haze has covered parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore for weeks as Jakarta struggles to contain fires that have scorched large tracts of Borneo and Sumatra, with the smoke drifting across the region. (Photo by Yuichi YAMAZAKI / AFP via Getty Images)Yuichi Yamazaki | Afp | Getty ImagesShares of several Singapore-listed agricultural companies fell Tuesday after Senior Minister K Shanmugam warned they won't "escape responsibility" for their possible role in the haze blanketing the city-state. "Companies cannot play hide and seek" with different corporate structures, hoping that will help them, Shanmugam said, revealing that seven companies had been questioned by the Singapore Exchange.Bumitama Agri fell as much as 6.5%, while First Resources dropped to a low of 4.83%. Golden Agri Resources and Wilmar International slipped almost 2%. We will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters, including on their bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors.K ShanmugamSenior Minister, SingaporeShanmugam, who is also home affairs minister for the city-state, said that some of the fires or smoke source points seem to be associated with First Resources, Bumitama Agri, as well as non-listed First Borneo Plantations. "Take, for example, First Resources. It issued a detailed statement on its zero burning policy and firefighting efforts ... but statements, no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Show us the evidence."The other companies named by the minister were Golden Agri-Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri and TSH Resources.The haze has affected businesses and daily life in Singapore and Malaysia in the past few weeks, with the air quality in Singapore hitting levels not seen since 2015. Schools in the state of Johor Bahru in Malaysia have also closed due to the air quality reaching unhealthy levels. "They should not underestimate the Singapore government's determination to act," Shanmugam said, adding, "we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters, including on their bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors."He also revealed that Singapore could even amend laws or introduce new laws "on an urgent basis" to ensure cooperation, if needed. Companies potentially linked to the haze would also be examined if they still meet the standards for government grants or incentives. 'Shiver in our shoes?'When asked if Singapore's actions will affect bilateral relations between the city-state and Jakarta, Shanmugam dismissed the concern, saying, "Our people are suffering. What do these experts think we are supposed to do? Shiver in our shoes before we take any action to protect our own people? That's not the Singapore approach."He was responding to a question about an article published by local media outlet CNA, which cited legal experts saying that actions taken by Singapore against haze-causing firms in Indonesia may carry diplomatic implications. "If we think like that, there will be no Singapore, and we do not think there should be any bilateral issues. The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interests as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems." He said that Singapore's actions against companies are aligned with the broad policies of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto. "In fact, we hope to get full cooperation from Indonesia in going after the companies," Shanmugam added

schema.headline: 'Cannot play hide and seek': Minister's warning over haze sends Singapore agricultural stocks lower

title: Top venture capitalist Jenny Lee says Asian startups are speeding toward IPOs
description: Jenny Lee, senior managing partner at Granite Asia, during the Bloomberg Invest summit in Hong Kong, China, on Wednesday, June 10, 2026. Bloomberg | B
body: Jenny Lee, senior managing partner at Granite Asia, during the Bloomberg Invest summit in Hong Kong, China, on Wednesday, June 10, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNewly formed companies are reaching the initial public offering stage far sooner than they used to, according to venture capitalist Jenny Lee.In the West, companies like to stay private a little longer, but Asian firms are leaning toward a more accelerated timeline, according to Lee, senior managing partner at Granite Asia and the first woman to break into the top 10 of the Forbes Global 100 VC Midas list. "On average the holding period before a company goes public is eight to 10 years," Lee said in an interview on the sidelines of the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference last week in Singapore. "But currently, the later stage companies we are seeing are actually preparing for IPOs when they are four to five years old."Investment platform Granite Asia works with startups from their first round through public listings, and in both equity and credit. Lee said the firm has made more than 40 equity investments in the last two years."At the very early stage ... we do see a lot more funding activity," Lee said. She added that companies in later stages of investment are seeing productivity gains and getting profitable faster.Granite Asia is concentrating on areas including artificial intelligence for science, and robotics, Lee said. It is also interested in concepts around Asian subcultures such as apps that would appeal in India specifically, or AI tools that help create Japanese content.Also, "we are looking at companies that have energy-related technology, say in storage, to help with the energy issue," she said. "Many of the countries in Asia import a huge percentage of their energy needs, and so as the countries grow onto a path to adopt more renewables, it's then important to have storage technology."

schema.headline: Top venture capitalist Jenny Lee says Asian startups are speeding toward IPOs

title: Tech stocks had a nice oversold bounce on Monday. Earnings this week will determine if it's for real
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on Oct. 14, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesT
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on Oct. 14, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesThis week's major earnings hold the key to whether this technology comeback has legs, investors said.The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite rallied Monday, largely due to a rebound in artificial intelligence  companies. Chip stocks surged, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) on pace to snap a nine-day slump. The Magnificent Seven outperformed, as did memory chip makers. The iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), dominated by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, surged 4% after also suffering steep declines over the past week. That comes after the S&P 500 fell nearly 2% last week, its worst weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.5% over the same five-day span. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNasdaq Composite, YTDMonday looked like a bounce from oversold conditions, but a bigger move will depend on this week's big tech earnings — which include results from major names such as Meta Platforms and Tesla — to clear some of the recent worries about the sustainability of the AI trade. SpaceX reports after the bell Tuesday."Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration," wrote Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays.This week will be especially crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support so as not to confirm a further breakdown, Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, said in a Monday note. For the time being, however, widespread, short-term oversold conditions suggest support can hold, she said.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconS&P 500, YTDEarnings test Of the 47 S&P 500 companies that have reported their third quarter thus far, 85% have beaten expectations, and the broad market index is on track to post a blended earnings growth rate of 29%.But the bulk of tech results are still to come, and they have a high bar to clear. "Investors are going to need proof statements from any company that is considered part of the AI trade that they can deliver on the earnings growth expectations being built into their pricing," said Ron Albahary, chief investment officer at LNW. "We don't have a valuation-potential bubble here like we had in the internet bubble. We have an earnings-expectation-potential bubble in this cycle."As a result, the market will take a "more discriminating" approach to tech, which Albahary views as a healthy move that will lead to "more of a dispersion of winners and losers within the AI trade universe." In that environment, some AI beneficiaries may continue to rise, while others like the neocloud platforms may sell off due to the amount of debt they're taking on to finance the build-out, he said. "Previously, the AI headlines would drive the bulk of the AI universe stocks up or down," the CIO said. "I don't think we're going to see that kind of uniformity going forward."As it stands now, action in the AI trade appears to be more of a "reality check" than a "full-blown unraveling," according to Wells Fargo Investment Institute's Sameer Samana. But he still believes there may be more pressure in the days and maybe even weeks ahead. "We recently downgrade[d] tech because we thought expectations had gotten too optimistic, and while the recent selling has taken some of that optimism out of the equation, we don't think it's fully done and may last through the midterms given the politicization of AI/data centers," the Wells Fargo head of global equities and real assets told CNBC.

schema.headline: Tech stocks had a nice oversold bounce on Monday. Earnings this week will determine if it's for real

title: U.S. Treasury yields move lower as investors await housing, employment data
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Sept. 16, 2026.Timothy A. Clary | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. Treasury yields inched lower on Tue
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Sept. 16, 2026.Timothy A. Clary | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. Treasury yields inched lower on Tuesday as investors awaited further economic data and continued to weigh the inflationary backdrop ahead of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next week. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was down 2 basis points to 5.114%, while the 30-year Treasury bond also fell 2 basis points to 5.45%. Meanwhile, the 2-year Treasury note yield was broadly flat at 4.757%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.Investors will parse housing starts and monthly pending home sales data for September, due later on Tuesday morning, and weekly ADP employment change figures. Weekly initial jobless claims will be released on Thursday, and the S&P Global Composite PMI Flash will be out on Friday. Investors are anticipating the Fed's next interest rate decision, due next week. The latest figures for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures index, will also be released. Traders are now pricing in an 82% chance of the Fed holding interest rates steady, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

schema.headline: U.S. Treasury yields move lower as investors await housing, employment data

title: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
description: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters i
body: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, April 30, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAnthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported.The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs."Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

schema.headline: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption

title: Trump says he'd meet with Putin and Xi, criticizes Zelenskyy
description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on Oct. 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesPresident D
body: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on Oct. 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump said Monday that he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss how to end the Ukraine war, while ramping up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Trump suggested that a meeting between the world leaders, which Putin reportedly proposed, could take place without Zelenskyy present."Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump told reporters when asked about the potential meeting as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.The comments came as tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy have steadily risen in recent weeks, while Russia — which invaded Ukraine in 2022 — has received multiple breaks from the U.S.Trump had initially suggested that he would be more interested in discussing "denuclearization" with Putin and Xi, saying, "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."The Wall Street Journal had reported that Putin in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump floated the idea of a trilateral summit with Xi next month.That meeting could take place at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, which is set for Nov. 18 and Nov. 19, the Journal reported."If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too. But yeah, I would do that," Trump said in Monday's remarks.He also said that Russia and China, which have both been accused of supporting Iran in its ongoing military efforts against the U.S., have done "very little" for Tehran. And when asked about Zelenskyy's criticism of Trump's recent decision to waive new sanctions against Russia — and his recent claim that Trump is on the wrong side of history — the U.S. president once again lashed out at the Ukrainian leader."Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said. "Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago.""I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump added, echoing his prior call for Kyiv to "get a new president."Zelenskyy says that Starlink and Starshield, the critical satellite services offered by Elon Musk's SpaceX, have recently been degraded, and that U.S. intelligence sharing has also been disrupted, leaving Ukraine without advance warning of Russian strikes.  "No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," Zelenskyy said earlier Monday after a call with bipartisan U.S. lawmakers from the House and Senate.Trump said outside the White House that he does not know who ordered the interruption to the Starlink service, "But I'd like to find out."Musk said last week that the U.S. government and Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the U.S. caused the interruption, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Zelenskyy to be "very careful about making statements like this that aren't true."Zelenskyy also once again criticized Trump's decision to waive key provisions of a new Russian sanctions bill, which was signed last month after passing Congress with broad bipartisan support.He said he showed the lawmakers photos from the scene of a Russian attack in the Kharkiv region that killed six people, including a mother and her 1-year-old child."This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the easing of pressure," Zelenskyy said.Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a joint statement after the meeting, "Funding Russia's war machine, disabling Ukraine's satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace.""Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties," the senators said.Trump had already been criticized by members of both parties after announcing a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel on the global market, despite existing sanctions.But in Monday's remarks, Trump pushed back, saying he is "not looking to break up negotiations" with Putin on deals pertaining to Ukraine, Iran, diesel and the release of hostages.

schema.headline: Trump says he'd meet with Putin and Xi, criticizes Zelenskyy

title: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction
description: Copper is becoming increasingly strategic to governments and industries as artificial intelligence, power-grid investment and defense spending increas
body: Copper is becoming increasingly strategic to governments and industries as artificial intelligence, power-grid investment and defense spending increase demand for the industrial metal, investors say.The metal — a key component in electronics, construction and transportation, and often seen as a barometer of economic activity — has outperformed gold this year, as the need to secure reliable supplies has intensified.watch nowCopper has rallied 15.8% year-to-date, and is up more than 30% over the past 12 months. By comparison, gold futures have slipped 4.11% year-to-date, and are down 4.52% over the past 12 months. Spot gold is 4.89% lower over the past 12 months, and 4% down year-to-date.Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin said countries, regions and industries are increasingly focused on securing access to metals for national security, economic growth and technology infrastructure. Melvin said that shift has helped support copper prices."It's certainly a good time to be in copper mining globally, and specifically in the United States," said Melvin, whose Arizona-based mining and exploration company focuses on copper, gold, silver, nickel and cobalt."We're really in a world right now where the metals that we used to refer to, and still do, as critical metals are really becoming strategic metals, in every sense of the word," said Melvin, who spoke as LME Week, the annual gathering of the global metals industry, began in London on Monday.AI and defense demandThat shift comes as investors question the sustainability of AI spending and the hyperscaler build-out, which has led to a recent wobble in tech stocks.But Melvin said he expects copper to withstand the recent volatility.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCopper."It's a new pocket of demand, and it really is almost an inelastic demand for copper," he said of the tech sector's need for the metal. "It's hard to think that one of these large-scale technology companies is going to make an investment decision on a hyperscale data center based on the cost of copper."He added: "That same inelasticity applies to another demand pocket that's emerging, which is national security, national defense budgets. So when you look at copper demand, the impact of technology, artificial intelligence infrastructure, I think we can all agree that that market is growing."There certainly has been a bit of a retrench, a retreat, in those [tech] valuations. But two things can be true at the same time — you can have a capital market move in sentiment on equity values… but it can also be true that those industries are growing, and they're going to be a source of incremental demand for our metal."U.S. copper tariffsThe rally has also been supported by uncertainty over whether the U.S. will impose a tariff on refined copper. In 2025, the Commerce Department recommended a 15% tariff beginning Jan. 1, 2027, but no final decision on the proposed levy has been publicly announced.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconGold."Because of the potential for US tariffs, a large share of the world's copper is now stored in the U.S., and it isn't clear those stocks will be available to the rest of the market," said Iain Pyle, senior investment director at Aberdeen Investments and co-manager of the abrdn Future Minerals Fund."At the same time, Chinese inventories look exceptionally low and premiums there are rising."In an Oct. 15 note, Pyle called copper the "clearest example" of a market where supply cannot keep up with demand. "Higher incentives will be needed in the form of sustained higher copper prices."There is still some risk of a pullback around tariff announcements, but we see the underlying fundamentals as clearly bullish, and the potential for a spike in prices has increased."

schema.headline: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction

title: Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to hike after MSCI threat fuels market rout
description: Destry Damayanti, governor of Bank Indonesia, during a news conference with Suahasil Nazara, Indonesia's finance minister, at the central bank's headq
body: Destry Damayanti, governor of Bank Indonesia, during a news conference with Suahasil Nazara, Indonesia's finance minister, at the central bank's headquarters in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to raise interest rates on Wednesday as economists revise their forecasts after global index provider MSCI warned it may downgrade the country's stock market from emerging-market status, setting off a selloff in stocks and the rupiah.Citibank now expects a pre-emptive 50 basis-point increase to 6.25%, abandoning its earlier call for no change. Capital Economics and Permata Bank expect a 25 basis-point hike to 6%. The central bank has held its benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate at 5.75% since June. MSCI said Friday it is considering moving Indonesia to "standalone" from the emerging-market status it has held since 1989, causing the Jakarta Composite Index to suffer the worst two-day sell-off recorded, before recovering about 3% Tuesday after authorities announced steps to improve market transparency and price discovery, including expelling tightly held companies from the flagship index. Meanwhile, rupiah weakened to 18,030 per dollar on Tuesday, near its June record low, falling about 8% this year. "Not delivering a rate hike [on Wednesday] would run the risk of disappointing investors and fueling further downward pressure on the currency," said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. "A decision to hold rates on Wednesday could also revive concerns among investors that Bank Indonesia is kowtowing to political pressure."Citi's Helmi Arman said a hike would aim to stop equity outflows spilling into bonds and prompting capital flight by domestic investors. He expects it to be a "one-off" followed by other support such as government foreign-currency borrowing or another round of bilateral currency swaps with foreign central banks.The central bank has already raised rates by a combined 100 basis points since May. Headline inflation quickened to a three-month high of 3.28% in September, within the 1.5%-3.5% target range, while core inflation eased to 2.84%. The governor, Destry Damayanti, has said foreign-exchange reserves of $146.3 billion at the end of September would be adequate to stabilize the rupiah.  Market integrity in question"Market confidence can deteriorate much faster than economic fundamentals," said Josua Pardede, chief economist at PT Bank Permata, estimating that foreign investors have net sold about $5 billion of Indonesian stocks this year. The risk is that foreign equity withdrawals could further weaken the rupiah and trigger selling in government bonds, he added. The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital.Josua PardedeChief economist, PT Bank PermataAn MSCI downgrade could force $3 billion to $5 billion of passive outflows, with another $15 billion of actively managed foreign money exposed to reassessment, he estimates. Pardede expects the market adjustment may come in stages, from precautionary selling through the first half of 2027 and mechanical selling if MSCI confirms the move by June. "BI can provide liquidity and reduce excessive volatility, but only credible market-governance reforms can address MSCI's fundamental concerns," he said, calling for credible free-float data, ownership disclosure and transparent engagement with international institutional investors. "The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital." watch now

schema.headline: Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to hike after MSCI threat fuels market rout

title: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop
description: Apple CEO John Ternus during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Ima
body: Apple CEO John Ternus during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesApple announced a product launch event on Oct. 28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles." The email says "Pro and tell," suggesting the launch will focus on high-end "Pro" devices with powerful homegrown chips. Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall. He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.Apple's invite to media for the event. AppleIt will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.Apple updated its Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktops with new chips in August, and refreshed its MacBook Pro in the spring, along with a new low-cost MacBook Neo. But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024. In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones. Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors. Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500. Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. schema.headline: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop

title: France curfews calm unrest as Macron faces criticism over Gulf trip
description: Protestors on the statue of Marianne on the Monument à la République (Statue de la République) during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, Fra
body: Protestors on the statue of Marianne on the Monument à la République (Statue de la République) during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France. Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesCurfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend's mass protests, looting and violent scenes. Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors.The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and a mounting fiscal crisis that threatens to turn into a sovereign debt crisis as government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades.The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027.In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required. Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years.Riots followed weeks of demonstrations amid public anger over the country's education system, the cost of living and other issues.While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire.Protesters vandalise a retail store during a demonstration near Paris's Place de la République, as the Gilets Jaunes join students for a weekend of action on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France.Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesPolitical commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in a scathing editorial that Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis." Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation.French assets came under pressure on Monday after the weekend scenes, with bonds, stocks and the euro all selling off, amid growing skepticism about the country's ability to bring down its deficit to a sustainable level. Fierce debate is underway over the 2027 budget, with the government targeting an overall decline in the deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%.

schema.headline: France curfews calm unrest as Macron faces criticism over Gulf trip

title: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
description: LONDON, ENGLAND - JULY 7: Deputy Governor for Financial Stability, Sarah Breeden, attends the Bank of England financial stability report press confere
body: LONDON, ENGLAND - JULY 7: Deputy Governor for Financial Stability, Sarah Breeden, attends the Bank of England financial stability report press conference at Bank Of England on July 7, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Doug Peters - WPA Pool/Getty Images)Wpa Pool | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesHedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday.Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress.watch now"One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an interview Thursday."It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was."Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconU.S. 10-Year Treasurys.Hedge fund assets swellWith gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday.  In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency.But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil. That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF. "The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said.Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market — particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt. Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19. Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-Year OATs.Earlier this month, 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on 10-year U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs.Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about the country's fiscal outlook — fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.

schema.headline: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
